content.p: Sobane Da is a small Dogon farming village in the Mopti region of central Mali. On the evening of Sunday 9 June 2019, armed men on motorbikes and pickup trucks surrounded it, set fire to its homes and storehouses and shot or cut down the people who ran. The assault lasted about seven hours, according to survivors. By the time it ended, the village had lost roughly a third of its inhabitants, in the BBC's estimate, and many of its houses.

The number of dead became a dispute of its own. Officials first said 95 people had been killed and 19 were missing. Two days later the government revised that to 35, 24 of them children, and said the first figure had added the dead and the missing together. The district mayor still insisted the true toll was higher. No group claimed the attack, no conviction has been reported, and its place in a wider cycle of Dogon and Fulani violence has made its causes a matter of argument.
content.h2: A region already at war with itself
content.p: Central Mali had been sliding toward communal violence for four years. After a predominantly Fulani jihadist movement led by the preacher Amadou Koufa appeared in 2015, the Fulani, who are mostly herders, came under suspicion from the farming communities around them, the Dogon and the Bambara. Dogon and Bambara villagers formed their own self-defence militias. Both sides accused the other of killing civilians. The Dogon accused the Fulani of supporting al-Qaeda-linked groups, NPR reported, while the Fulani said the Malian military was arming Dogon hunters against them.

Disputes over land, water and grazing were old, but analysts described them as hardened by the insecurity. Paul Melly of the think tank Chatham House told Al Jazeera that jihadist preaching had added an ideological edge, and that a large number of killings had fed mistrust and bitterness. Baba Dakono, of the Institute for Security Studies in Bamako, said that the militias had been created, rightly or wrongly, to answer a need for security among people who had lost faith in the state.

The weeks before Sobane Da were bloody. On 16 May the United Nations mission in Mali, MINUSMA, said it had recorded at least 488 deaths in attacks on Fulani people in the Mopti and Segou regions since January 2018. It also said armed Fulani had caused 63 civilian deaths in Mopti over the same period. The worst single attack was on 23 March at Ogossagou, where at least 157 civilians were killed, according to NPR, by suspected Dogon hunters. A Dogon militia leader denied that his group was responsible. The Ogossagou killings forced the prime minister's resignation and led the government to ban the Dogon militia Dan Na Ambassagou, which says it is a self-defence group and refused to disarm. Human Rights Watch later wrote that the government pledged to dissolve and disarm the militia and failed to do so.

Accounts of the hour differ. The government's first statement, reported by the BBC, said "suspected terrorists" attacked at around 03:00. Survivors and the UN mission said the assault began on Sunday evening, and a community leader told Human Rights Watch that the attackers came at 5 p.m. on many motorcycles that quickly surrounded the village.

A survivor who gave his name as Amadou Togo told AFP that about 50 heavily armed men arrived on motorbikes and pickups. "They first surrounded the village and then attacked, anyone who tried to escape was killed," he said. He described people with their throats cut or disembowelled and grain stores and cattle set alight. The village chief, Gouno Dara, who escaped, told AFP that the assailants opened fire on anything that moved. He said they shouted "Allahu Akbar", then burned the storehouses and homes and took sheep and cattle. "We have nothing left," he said. A farmer in his thirties, Jean Dara, told reporters that he had lost his wife, two sons, a daughter and both of his parents.

Human Rights Watch interviewed three witnesses, two of whom said they recognised several attackers as men from neighbouring villages. A community leader told the organisation that the village, with 431 residents, was entirely Dogon and entirely Christian, yet the church was not burned, nor were houses with crosses on them. Human Rights Watch took that to suggest that religion was not the reason for the attack. The same community leader said most of those killed were children. The group counted more than 20 children among the 35 dead, and SBS reported the prime minister's statement that many had been shot in the back.

On Monday 10 June a local official told AFP that 95 civilians were dead and that the bodies were burned. The government gave the same figure with 19 people missing. A Malian security source at the site said the village had been "virtually wiped out". Identifying victims was hard, the BBC reported, because many houses had been burned down. On 11 June the district mayor, Ali Dolo, said that 108 people had been found safe and were sheltering in a school.

On Wednesday 12 June the government cut the toll to 35, which it said was the result of a painstaking count by civil protection officials, forensic doctors and the public prosecutor of Mopti. Eleven of the dead were adults and 24 were children. The statement said that about a hundred women had escaped to the village of Koundo, which was one cause of the confusion, and that the original 95 had been based on early information from soldiers and from the district mayor.

Dolo did not accept the change. The new figure left out charred remains not yet identified, he said, adding: "He has his toll, we have ours." Human Rights Watch later also gave 35 as the number of dead.

The government's first statement blamed "suspected terrorists". The mayor of nearby Bankass, Moulaye Guindo, told Reuters that Fulani men had attacked the village, and a local official told the BBC he believed Fulani people were responsible. Al Jazeera reported that a Dogon leader called the killings an act of war and said he believed Fulanis were responsible. The same broadcaster said Koufa's group had promised after Ogossagou that the Fulani would take revenge. Ousmane Diallo, a Malian researcher, said the details suggested "jihadist methods" but cautioned that the truth could be more complex and the motives were unclear.

The most detailed findings came from MINUSMA's human rights section, whose July 2019 report, as summarised by Human Rights Watch, concluded that the attack was carried out by 30 to 40 armed men, "described as young Peuhl men from surrounding villages". The investigators could not determine whether the attackers belonged to a particular group. Human Rights Watch listed Sobane Da among attacks allegedly carried out by Peuhl self-defence groups, and in its World Report said Peuhl militiamen were implicated.

President Ibrahim Boubacar Keita cut short a trip to Switzerland. "This country cannot be run by a cycle of revenge and vendetta," he told state television from Geneva. Prime Minister Boubou Cisse visited the village on 11 June. He had taken office in April after the Ogossagou massacre brought down his predecessor. The MINUSMA chief, Mahamat Saleh Annadif, called the attack "unspeakable barbarity" and said that "everybody is responsible" for the spiral of violence. Speaking at UN headquarters, he also said he regretted the thin presence of Malian authorities in the area, which had not prevented the violence. The UN secretary-general, Antonio Guterres, appealed to all parties to show restraint and avoid retaliation. A security expert quoted by News24, who was not named, noted that the army had been deployed about 20 kilometres from the village without being able to stop the attack.

The restraint the officials asked for did not hold. On 12 June, gunmen attacked two Dogon villages in the Bankass district, less than 50 kilometres away, and a local official and a security source said at least two people died. The following Monday, gunmen on motorbikes struck the villages of Gangafani and Yoro in the same region. Al Jazeera reported at least 38 deaths and quoted a survivor who said the gunmen accused residents of having cooperated with the Malian and Burkinabe military in an earlier raid. The International Committee of the Red Cross, which was preparing to bring aid to survivors of Sobane Da, said there had been four major attacks since the start of the year.

The government said on 12 June that six people had been detained following routine checks. Mali's Ministry of Justice announced on 10 June that the prosecutor of its Specialized Judicial Unit had opened an investigation. By October 2019, Human Rights Watch reported, at least nine suspects were in pretrial detention on the order of the unit's investigating judge. Human Rights Watch said the unit, which handles terrorism and organised crime, had two communal violence cases among its files: Ogossagou and Sobane Da. MINUSMA's human rights staff and judicial advisers supported its investigations into both.

No trial or verdict in the case has been reported. In its 2020 world report, Human Rights Watch said there was scant progress on justice for atrocities in Mali since 2012 and 2013, and that local groups said officials shied away from questioning or charging militia leaders who were credibly implicated, preferring short-term reconciliation to ease communal tension. The village's survivors, by the community leader's account, had all fled.
